title: Question
body_md: Can it be proved, without the use of the continuum hypothesis, that there exists a complete theory having exactly $\aleph_1$ non-isomorphic denumerable models?
head: environment

title: Conjecture
body_md: If a Polish group $G$ acts continuously on a Polish space $X$, then either there are countably many orbits, or there is a (non-empty) perfect subset of $X$ whose distinct points lie in distinct orbits.

name: Topological Vaught Conjecture

title: Definition
body_md:
Suppose $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a$ is a language where, for each $n \geq 1$, the language $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a^n$ has a unique relation symbol $P_n$. We define the {\bf{theory of $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a$-geometry}} to be the countable theory $
\operatorname{Th}_{\operatorname{Geo}}(#1)
[\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a] \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}_{\omega_1, \ensuremath{\omega}}(\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a)$ consisting of the following sentences. 
\begin{itemize}
\item For $n \geq 1$,  
\[
(\forall x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})\, P_n(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \rightarrow \bigwedge_{i < j \in [n]} (x_i \neq x_j)
\]
and if $\sigma\: [n] \to [n]$ is a bijection then 
\[
(\forall x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})\, P_n(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \leftrightarrow P_n(x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)}).
\]

\item For all $n \geq 1$,
\[
(\forall x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})\bigwedge_{i < j \in [n]} (x_i \neq x_j) \rightarrow \bigvee_{k \in \ensuremath{\omega}}(\exists x_n, \dots, x_{n+k -1})\, P_{n+k}(x_0, \dots, x_{n+k-1}).
\]

\item For $n_0, n_1, k\geq 1$ if $P_{n_0}(x_0, \dots, x_{n_0-1})$ and $P_{n_1}(y_0, \dots, y_{n_1-1})$ and $z_0, \dots, z_{k-1}$ is an enumeration of $\{x_i\}_{i \in [n_0]} \cap \{y_i\}_{i \in [n_1]}$ then $P_k(z_0, \dots, z_{k-1})$ holds. 
\end{itemize}

If $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$ is an $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}$-structure which satisfies $
\operatorname{Th}_{\operatorname{Geo}}(#1)
[\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a]$ then we say ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$ has a {\bf{$\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a$-geometry}} and we call a tuple satisfying a relation in $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a$ {\bf{closed}}.

title: Definition
body_md:
Suppose that
\begin{itemize}

\item $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a, \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b, \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c$ are languages with $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c \cap \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b =\emptyset$ and $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c$, and

\item for each $n \geq 1$, we have $|\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a^n| = 1$ and $|\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b^n| > 0$. 
\end{itemize}
We define the theory of {\bf{$(\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a, \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b, \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c)$-structured geometry}}, denoted by $
\operatorname{Th}_{\operatorname{SGeo}}(#1, #2, #3)
<\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a>[\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b](\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c)$, to consist of the following collections of sentences.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] $
\operatorname{Th}_{\operatorname{Geo}}(#1)
[\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a]$.

\item[(b)] For all $n \geq 1$ and $P_n \in \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a^n$,
\[
(\forall x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})\, P_n(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \leftrightarrow \bigvee_{Q_n \in \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b^n} Q_n(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}).
\]

\item[(c)] For all $n \geq 1$ and distinct $Q_n, Q_n'\in \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b^n$, 
\[
(\forall x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})\, Q_n(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \rightarrow \neg Q_n'(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}).
\]

\item[(d)] For any $k, n \geq 1$, any $Q \in \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b^n$,  any $R \in \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b^k \cup \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c^k$, and any sequence $\<i_j\>_{j \in [k]} \subseteq [n]$,
\begin{align*}
(\forall x_0,\dots, x_{n-1})&(\forall y_0, \dots, y_{n-1})\, [Q(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})  \ensuremath{\wedge} Q(y_0, \dots, y_{n-1})]  \\
 
&\rightarrow [R(x_{i_0}, \dots, x_{i_{k-1}}) \leftrightarrow R(y_{i_0}, \dots, y_{i_{k-1}})].
\end{align*}
\end{itemize}

If $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a, \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b, \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$ is an $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}$-structure which satisfies $
\operatorname{Th}_{\operatorname{SGeo}}(#1, #2, #3)
<\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a>[\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b](\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c)$ then we say that ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$ has an {\bf{$(\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a, \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b, \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c)$-structured geometry}}. 

We call elements of $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b$ {\bf{invariants}}. If ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}\models 
\operatorname{Th}_{\operatorname{SGeo}}(#1, #2, #3)
<\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a>[\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b](\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c)$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \models Q({\ensuremath{\mathbf{a}}})$ where $Q \in \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b$ then we call $Q$ the {\bf{invariant}} of ${\ensuremath{\mathbf{a}}}$. We also refer to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$ as a {\bf{lift}} of ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}\ensuremath{\!\upharpoonright_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c}}$.

body_md:
Suppose $\mathcal{I}$ is an invariant diagram and $\ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{\tau}}} = \<\tau_\beta\>_{\beta \in \ensuremath{\omega}_1}$ is an invariant system. We say that $\mathcal{I}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{\tau}}}$ are {\bf{compatible}} if for all $\beta \in \ensuremath{\omega}_1$, 
\begin{itemize}
\item if $(P({\bm{x}}), Q({\bm{y}})) \in \mathcal{I}$ with $P, Q \in \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b$ then $(\tau_\beta(P)({\bm{x}}), \tau_\beta(Q)({\bm{y}})) \in \mathcal{I}$, and 

\item if $P \in \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b$ and $Q \in \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c$ then 
\[
(P({\bm{x}}), Q({\bm{y}})) \in \mathcal{I} \text{ if and only if }(\tau_\beta(P)({\bm{x}}), Q({\bm{y}})) \in \mathcal{I}.
\]
\end{itemize}

label: Countably many equiv-beta classes implies no perfect set
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Countably many equiv-beta classes implies no perfect set}
Suppose $\Phi$ is a class of geometric $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c$-structures closed under isomorphism such that for all $\beta \in \ensuremath{\omega}_1$, all $\equiv_\beta$-antichains in $\Phi$ are countable. Then there does not exist a perfect set of non-isomorphic models in $\Phi$.
head: environment
labels: Countably many equiv-beta classes implies no perfect set

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose to get a contradiction that there is a perfect set $P$ of non-isomorphic models in $\Phi$. Let $BO$ be the collection of codes for countable linear orders $(L, \leq)$ such that there are distinct ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{N}}} \in P$ and a sequence $\<I_i\>_{i \in L}$ which satisfy the conditions of \cref{Back and forth system definition}, each element of which is non-empty. If $L$ is ill-founded then by a standard back and forth argument we must have ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \cong {\ensuremath{\mathcal{N}}}$. Therefore, because no two elements of $P$ are isomorphic, any linear order in $BO$ must be well-founded.  

But $BO$ is a $\Sigma_1^1$-class as the conditions in \cref{Back and forth system definition} are Borel in an appropriate space. So by $\Sigma_1^1$-bounding \cite[Corollary~25.14]{MR1940513} there must be a $\gamma < \ensuremath{\omega}_1$ such that all orders in $BO$ have order type at most $\gamma$. Therefore if ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{N}}} \in P$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \equiv_{\gamma+1} {\ensuremath{\mathcal{N}}}$ we must have ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} = {\ensuremath{\mathcal{N}}}$. Hence $P$ is an antichain in $\equiv_{\gamma+1}$. But $|P| = 2^\ensuremath{\omega}$, getting us our contradiction.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\beta \in \ensuremath{\omega}_1$. Let 
\[
A_\beta = \{{\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \in K_{-\infty} \,:\, (\forall {\ensuremath{\mathcal{N}}} \in K_\beta)\, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{N}}} \ensuremath{\!\upharpoonright_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c}} \neq {\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}\}.
\]
By (b) $A_\beta$ has only countably many isomorphism classes. 

For ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{N}}} \in K_\beta$ define ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \sim {\ensuremath{\mathcal{N}}}$ if there is some $Q \in \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b$ such that ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \models (\exists {\bm{x}})\, Q({\bm{x}})$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{N}}} \models (\exists {\bm{x}})\, Q({\bm{x}})$. Note that every relation symbol in $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b$ which is realized in a structure in $K_\beta$ must have rank at most $\beta$ and hence be in $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b[\ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{\tau}}}, \beta]$. But $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b[\ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{\tau}}}, \beta]$ is countable and so any $\sim$-antichain must be countable. 

By the definition of $A_\beta$, any model ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \in K_{-\infty}\setminus A_\beta$ must have a lift ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}^* \in K_\beta$.  By \cref{Knight systems imply equiv-beta equivalence} if $B$ is a $\equiv_\beta$-antichain among elements of $K_{-\infty} \setminus A_\beta$ then there must be an $\sim$-antichain $B^+$  such that $B = \{{\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}\ensuremath{\!\upharpoonright_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c}} \,:\, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \in B^+\}$. Therefore every $\equiv_\beta$-antichain in $K_{-\infty}\setminus A_\beta$ must be countable. Hence, because $A_\beta$ is countable up to isomorphism, any $\equiv_\beta$-antichain in $K_{-\infty}$ must be countable as well. But then by \cref{Countably many equiv-beta classes implies no perfect set}, $K_{-\infty}$ does not contain a perfect set of non-isomorphic models.

title: Definition
body_md:
Suppose $\ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{K}}} = \<K_\beta\>_{\beta \in \ensuremath{\omega}_1}$ is a weak Knight system (for $(\mathcal{I}, \ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{\tau}}})$) and $\beta\in \ensuremath{\omega}_1$. We say that ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \in K_\beta$ is {\bf{maximal at level $\beta$}} (for $\ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{K}}}$) if whenever $\beta^* > \beta$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}^* \in K_{\beta^*}$ and $\tau_{\beta}({\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}^*) = {\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$, then ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} = {\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}^*$. We say that ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$ is {\bf{maximal}} if it is maximal at some level. 

We say $\ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{K}}}$ {\bf{has few maximal models}} if for all $\beta \in \ensuremath{\omega}_1$, up to isomorphism, there are countably many models which are maximal at $\beta$.

\label{Knight class definition}
We say a collection $\Phi$ of $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c$-structures is a {\bf{Knight class}} if there is an invariant diagram $\mathcal{I}$, a compatible invariant system $\ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{\tau}}} = \<\tau_\beta\>_{\beta \in \ensuremath{\omega}_1}$, and a Knight system $\ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{K}}} = \<K_\beta\>_{\beta \in \ensuremath{\omega}_1}$ (for $(\mathcal{I}, \ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{\tau}}})$) such that $\Phi = K_{-\infty}$. We say that $\ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{K}}}$ {\bf{witnesses}} that $\Phi$ is a Knight class.

label: Knight sentences are counterexamples to Vaught's conjecture
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Knight sentences are counterexamples to Vaught's conjecture}
If $\sigma\in \ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}_{\omega_1, \ensuremath{\omega}}(\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c)$ is a Knight sentence then $\sigma$ has $\aleph_1$ many countable models up to isomorphism and does not have a perfect set of non-isomorphic models. Hence $\sigma$ is a counterexample to Vaught's conjecture for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}_{\omega_1, \ensuremath{\omega}}$.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a = \{P_n\}_{n \geq 1}$ where, for each $n \geq 1$, the relation symbol $P_n$ is of arity $n$. Let $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c = \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a \cup \{\leq\}$ where $\leq$ is a binary relation symbol. 

We say an $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c$-structure ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$ is a {\bf{geometric tree}} if it satisfies the following. 
\begin{itemize}
\item $\leq$ is a partial order with a greatest element called the root.  
\item For all $a \in {\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$, the set $\{a' \in {\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \,:\, a' \geq a\}$ is finite and linearly ordered. 

\item For $n \geq 1$, we have
\[
(\forall x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})\, P_n(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \leftrightarrow \bigg[\Bigl(\bigwedge_{i < j \in [n]} x_i \neq x_j\Bigr) \ensuremath{\wedge} (\forall y)\, \bigg[\Bigl(\bigvee_{i \in [n]} y \geq x_i \Bigr) \rightarrow \Bigl(\bigvee_{i \in [n]} y = x_i\Bigr)\bigg]\bigg].
\]
\end{itemize}

If ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$ is a geometric tree and $a, b \in {\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$, we will say ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \models a <_1 b$ if ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \models a < b$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \models (\forall c)\, a \leq c \leq b \rightarrow (c = a \ensuremath{\vee} c = b)$, i.e., $a$ is an immediate predecessor of $b$.

body_md:
By a {\bf{labeled tree}} we mean a pair $\<(T, \leq), \mu\>$ where 
\begin{itemize}
\item $(T, \leq)$ is a rooted tree, 

\item $\mu\:T \to \ensuremath{\omega}_1 \cup \{\infty\}$, 

\item for all $a < b \in T$, we have $\mu(a) < \mu(b)$, where $\infty < \infty$. 
\end{itemize}
We call $T$ the {\bf{underlying set}} of the labeled tree and we call $\mu$ the {\bf{labeling}}. We say that a labeled tree is {\bf{finite}} when its underlying set is.  

If $T_0 \subseteq T$ is an upwards closed set and $\mu_0 = \mu\ensuremath{\!\upharpoonright_{T_0}}$, then we say that $\<(T, \leq), \mu\>$ {\bf{extends}} \linebreak $\<(T_0, \leq\,\ensuremath{\!\upharpoonright_{T_0 \times T_0}}), \mu_0\>$.

title: Definition
body_md: For $n\geq 1$ let $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b^n = \{Q_\zeta \,:\, \zeta\text{ is a finite labeled tree with underlying set }[n]\}$.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{tr}}$ be the invariant diagram such that whenever $\zeta = \<([n], \leq), \mu\>$ is a finite labeled tree and $P \in \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b \cup \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c$ then $(Q_\zeta(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}), P(x_{i_0}, \dots, x_{i_{k-1}})) \in \mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{tr}}$ precisely when one of the following holds. 
\begin{itemize}
\item $P$ is $\leq$ and $i_0 \leq i_1$, 

\item $P$ is $P_k$, $i_0, \dots, i_{k-1}$ are distinct elements and $\{i_j\}_{j \in [k]}$ is an upwards closed set in $([n], \leq)$, 

\item $P$ is $Q_{\zeta^*}$ where $\zeta^* = \<([k], \leq_{\zeta^*}), \nu\>$, the map $i_\ell \mapsto \ell$ is an isomorphism between $([n], \leq_\zeta)\ensuremath{\!\upharpoonright_{\{i_j\}_{j \in [k]}}}$ and $([k], \leq_{\zeta^*})$, the sequence $\{i_j\}_{j \in [k]}$ is upwards closed, and 
$\nu(j) = \mu(i_j)$
for all $j \in [k]$. 
\end{itemize}
We call a structure compatible with $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{tr}}$ a {\bf{labeled geometric tree}}.

Suppose ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}$ is a plan on $A$. A {\bf{graded face}} for ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}$ is a pair $(B, j)$ such that $B \in {\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}$ and $1 \leq j \leq |B|$. We let $
\mathfrak{GF}(#1)
[{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}]$ be the collection of graded faces for ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}$. 

If $(B, j)$ is a graded face, we call $B$ the {\bf{scope}} and $j$ the {\bf{grade}}. We let $s_{{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}}\:
\mathfrak{GF}(#1)
[{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}] \to {\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}$ be the map which takes a graded face and returns its scope and we let $g_{{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}}\: 
\mathfrak{GF}(#1)
[{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}] \to \ensuremath{\omega}$ be the map which takes a graded face and returns its grade. If $(B_0, j_0), (B_1, j_1) \in 
\mathfrak{GF}(#1)
[{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}]$ then we say $(B_0, j_0) \leq (B_1, j_1)$ if $B_0 \subseteq B_1$ and $j_0 \leq j_1$.

title: Definition
body_md:
A {\bf{frame}} on a plan ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}$ is a map $c\:D \to 
\mathfrak{GF}(#1)
[{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}]$.  We call the elements of $D$ the {\bf{cells}} of the frame and define the scope of a cell $d$ to be $s_{{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}}(c(d))$ and the  grade of a cell $d$ to be $g_{{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}}(c(d))$. We will abuse notation and write $s_{{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}}(d)$ for $s_{{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}}(c(d))$ and $g_{{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}}(d)$ for $g_{{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}}(c(d))$. 

If $U \in 
\mathfrak{GF}(#1)
[{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}]$ we let $D \downarrow U = \{d \in D \,:\, (s(d), g(d)) \leq U\}$. For $d \in D$ we let $D \downarrow d = D \downarrow c(d)$.

A {\bf{template}} for ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}$ is a triple $t = (c, \Sigma, p)$ where $c$ is a frame for ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}$,  where $\Sigma = (\ell_d)_{d \in D}$ is a row system for $c$, and where $p$ is a label for $c$. 

We define the {\bf{range}} of the template $t$ to be $\operatorname{range}(t) = \operatorname{range}(p)$. For $\alpha \in \ensuremath{\omega}_1$ we say that $t$ is an {\bf{$\alpha$-template}} if $\operatorname{range}(t) \subseteq \{-\infty\} \cup \alpha \cup \{\infty\}$.

Suppose $i\:A \to A^*$ is a bijection and ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}^* = \{i[B] \,:\, B \in {\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}\}$. 

\begin{itemize}
\item We say that $i$ is an {\bf{isomorphism from $(A, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}})$ to $(A^*, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}^*)$}}. 

\item Suppose $c\:D \to 
\mathfrak{GF}(#1)
[{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}]$ and $c^*\:D \to 
\mathfrak{GF}(#1)
[{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}^*]$ are frames. We say that $i$ is an {\bf{isomorphism from $c$ to $c^*$}} if $c^* = \hat{\imath} \circ c$ where $\hat{\imath}\:
\mathfrak{GF}(#1)
[{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}] \to 
\mathfrak{GF}(#1)
[{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}^*]$ is the map that takes $(B, j)$ to $(i[B], j)$.

\item Suppose $t = (c, \Sigma, p)$ and $t^* = (c^*, \Sigma, p)$ are templates. We say that $i$ is an {\bf{isomorphism from $t$ to $t^*$}} if it is an isomorphism from $c$ to $c^*$. 
\end{itemize}

Suppose $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a = \{P_n\}_{n \geq 1}$ where each $P_n$ has arity $n$. We say that an $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a$-structure ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$ is a {\bf{plan}} if ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \models 
\operatorname{Th}_{\operatorname{Geo}}(#1)
[\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_a]$ and $\{\emptyset\} \cup \bigcup_{n \geq 1} \bigl\{\{a_i\}_{i \in [n]} \,:\, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \models P_n(a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})\bigr\}$ is a plan.

title: Definition
body_md:
For $\beta \in \ensuremath{\omega}_1$, let $K_\beta[T]$ be the collection of $(\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b[T] \cup \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c[T])$-structures ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$ such that 
\begin{itemize}
\item ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$ is compatible with $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{temp}}[#1][T]$, 

\item $\tau_\beta({\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}) = {\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}$, and 

\item ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \models D[\alpha]$ for all $\alpha < \ensuremath{\omega} + \ensuremath{\omega} \cdot \beta$.
\end{itemize}
We let $\ensuremath{\mathop{\pmb{K}}}[T] = \<K_\beta[T]\>_{\beta \in \ensuremath{\omega}_1}$, let $K[T] = \bigcup_{\beta \in \ensuremath{\omega}_1} K_\beta[T]$ and let $K_{-\infty}[T] = \{{\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}}\ensuremath{\!\upharpoonright_{{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c[T]}}} \,:\, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{M}}} \in K[T]\}$.

title: Definition
body_md:
Suppose $t = (c, \Sigma, p)$ is a template over the plan $(A, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}})$ with $\Sigma = (\ell_d)_{d \in D}$. We say $t$ is {\bf{legal}} if it satisfies the following.  
\begin{itemize}

\item $\operatorname{range}(c) = 
\mathfrak{GF}(#1)
[{\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}}]$, i.e., every graded face has a cell.

\item $p$ is lawful with respect to $\Sigma$.

\item For each $d \in D$, $\ell_d$ is lawful.

\item The rows of $(\ell_d)_{d \in D}$ are bountiful.

\item For each $d$, $\operatorname{range}(\ell_d) \subseteq \{-\infty\} \cup \{\ensuremath{\omega} \cdot n + i \,:\, n \in \ensuremath{\omega}, i \leq g(d) + 1\}$. 

\end{itemize}

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $C_\beta[L]$ has only countably many isomorphism types the  existence of ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}}_\beta$ follows immediately from \cref{Charts have (HP) (JEP) (AP)} and the standard Fra\"{i}ss\'{e}\ construction.
The fact that ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}}_\beta \in K_\beta$ follows from the fact that the extension property of ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}}_\beta$ implies ${\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}}_\beta$ satisfies $D[\delta]$ for all $\delta < \ensuremath{\omega} + \ensuremath{\omega} \cdot \beta$.

label: Only countably many maximal structures at each level
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Only countably many maximal structures at each level}
For each $\beta$ there are only countably many $(\ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_b[L] \cup \ensuremath{\mathfrak{L}}_c[L])$-structures up to isomorphism that are maximal at $\beta$.
head: environment
labels: Only countably many maximal structures at each level

label: Knight sentence from legal template system
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Knight sentence from legal template system}
The sentence $\sigma[L]$ has $\aleph_1$ many countable models up to isomorphism and has no perfect set of non-isomorphic countable models. In particular, $\sigma[L]$ is a counterexample to Vaught's conjecture for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}_{\omega_1, \ensuremath{\omega}}$.
